title: Quietly working (2 Thessalonians 3:6–13)
hookLine: work quietly, eat your own bread, don't grow weary in doing well
carry: be not weary in well doing
tomorrow: is money really the root of all evil? read the whole line.

cards: Every group chat has one: the person with opinions on everyone's business who somehow never finishes their own. A second letter to Thessalonica names that exact problem.
Paul hears that some in the church are "working not at all, but are busybodies." Not idle and quiet. Busy, just not with their own work.
Busy with everybody else's. So what's the cure? Paul's answer starts with a memory.

teach.h: EAT NO MAN'S BREAD FOR NOUGHT.
teach.b: The memory: "Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you."
Paul and his companions paid their own way, he says, to give the church an example. Then the line people still quote: "if any would not work, neither should he eat." Read the verb closely.
Would not, not could not. It's about the able and unwilling, not the sick or anyone who can't find work.
Then the cure itself: "that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread." Quietness here isn't silence. It's minding your own work without hovering over everyone else's.
So that's Paul's answer: honest work, done quietly, is a kind of peace. A neighbor tradition prizes it too.

teach.h: GURU NANAK: EARN, AND GIVE SOME AWAY.
teach.b: In the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, Guru Nanak says that whoever eats what they earn by their own work, and gives some of it away, has recognized the path. Sikhs call honest work kirat karni.
Shared ground: your own bread, earned honestly. One honest difference: the Guru's line ties earning straight to giving some away; Paul's lines here tie it to quiet, and to not being a burden.

teach.h: BE NOT WEARY IN WELL DOING.
teach.b: Then Paul turns to the tired ones doing it right: "But ye, brethren, be not weary in well doing." Even his correction stays gentle: the one who won't listen, he says, is not an enemy but a brother.

how: Some Christians see ordinary, honest work done well as part of their faith, and some monastic communities join daily prayer with daily work.

o: working in secret so nobody can judge you
doing your own work without noise or meddling
never speaking up, even when something's wrong

s: 'if any would not work, neither should he eat' is about people who can't find work
the verb is would not: the able and unwilling, not the sick or those without work.
Paul says he paid his own way among the Thessalonians
"neither did we eat any man's bread for nought": he worked night and day, as an example.
Sikh scripture also prizes honest work, in its own words
Guru Nanak ties eating what you earn to giving some of it away (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245).

games.q: a classmate says 'if any would not work, neither should he eat' proves people who lose their jobs don't deserve help. what does the verse actually say?
o: would not: it's about the able and unwilling, not those who can't.
anyone without a job, for any reason, should go without.
it's about church leaders only, who shouldn't be paid at all.
games.why: the King James says would not, not could not. Paul is writing about people able to work who became busybodies instead.

practice: Choose one piece of honest work that's yours today, a task nobody else will do for you.
Name what finishing it well would look like, name the one thing most likely to pull you off it, and decide the first small step you'll take when the sit ends.
Keep that step small enough to do without anyone noticing, which is rather the point.

wordCard.voice: Quietly working. Paul's word to the Thessalonians: do your own work, without noise or meddling, and eat your own bread.

carryVoice: Keep this one: be not weary in well doing, said to the ones already doing the work. Until tomorrow.
